result.summary: Pindar celebrates Alkimedon of Aigina, a boy wrestler who won at Olympia in 460 B.C. He praises Aigina's justice and tells how Aiakos helped build Troy's wall and how Apollo read a sign of its fall. He praises trainer Melesias and the victor's family, and prays for their continued fortune.

scenes.title: Invocation of Olympia and Aigina
scenes.summary: Pindar addresses Olympia, announces the victory of Alkimedon, and praises Aigina's justice toward strangers.

scenes.title: Aiakos builds Troy's wall
scenes.summary: Aiakos helps Apollo and Poseidon build Troy's wall; three dragons assault it and Apollo interprets the sign as Troy's fall through Aiakos' descendants.
scenes.stakes: Troy's wall is destined to fall to Aiakos' descendants.

scenes.title: Praise of Melesias and the family
scenes.summary: Pindar defends himself against envy, praises the trainer Melesias and the Blepsiad family, and prays for their lasting prosperity.
scenes.stakes: Pindar and the family face envy and the risk of reversal of fortune.

Aphorism that noble deeds free a man from fear of death.

analysis.text: The ode links athletic victory to justice, divine favour and family glory, with Aigina's hospitality and heroic past as background.
Aigina was a major Greek naval power, and Pindar wrote many odes for its athletes, who often won in boys' events and trained under figures like Melesias.

fun_facts.text: Of Pindar's forty-four surviving victory odes, eleven honour Aiginetan winners.

language_notes.text: Diviners 'made trial of Zeus' by reading omens in burnt offerings (pyromancy) at Olympia, seeking a sign whether the god promised success to contestants.
Nemea and 'the hill of Kronos' (at Olympia) name the sites of two victories: Timosthenes won at the Nemean games, Alkimedon at Olympia.
'Of long oars' is a fixed descriptive phrase for Aigina, an island famed for seafaring. 'Stranger's succour' refers to Zeus as protector of guests.
Ilion is Troy. 'Make a crown for Ilion' means build its crowning wall; Aiakos' help was needed because a mortal had to share the work.
Pergamos was the citadel of Troy.
'First and fourth' means Aiakos' son Telamon (with Herakles, in the first sack) and his great-grandson Neoptolemos, in the later war; interpretations vary.
'Trident-wielder' is an epithet for Poseidon; Isthmos is the Isthmus of Corinth, where the Isthmian games were held.
Pindar hopes envy will not pelt him with 'a cruel stone', meaning malicious criticism for praising Melesias so much.
Pindar promises a further ode for a victory at Nemea, the games in the Nemean valley, won in the pankration, a combined wrestling and boxing contest.
'The loathed return ungreeted of fair speech' means going home defeated, with no words of praise to welcome the losers; 'striplings' are the youths defeated.
'Blepsiad' is the name of Alkimedon's clan, the Blepsiadai, descended from a common ancestor.
Iphion and Kallimachos are Alkimedon's dead father and grandfather. Fame, daughter of Hermes the messenger god, will carry the news to them in the underworld.
'Contrary discontent' means a reversal of fortune or divine resentment sent to balance the family's great success.

context_notes.text: 460 B.C. is the year of the 80th Olympiad, when the boy Alkimedon won the boys' wrestling.
Themis is the goddess of justice and established order; she sits beside Zeus. Aigina was famed for just dealing.
Aiakos, a legendary king of Aigina, was son of Zeus and famed for justice. Apollo (Leto's son) and Poseidon served Laomedon of Troy.
Xanthos is a river or region of Lycia, and Ister is the Danube; Apollo journeys to far northern and eastern lands.
Melesias was the Athenian trainer of Alkimedon, famous for coaching many young athletes to victory.
Greeks believed the dead could share in the honour of their living kin's victories, especially when praised in song and rites.

literary_notes.text: Pindar addresses Olympia directly as a mother and queen, making the sacred site a personified recipient of the victory.
Aigina becomes 'a pillar built of God,' a metaphor for the island as a firm support for strangers.
The three dragons stand for the fate of the wall: two fall, one enters, an omen of the city's capture.
Apollo's reading foretells Troy's fall at the hands of Aiakos' descendants, linking the myth to Aigina's heroic line.
Envy is imagined as a woman hurling a stone, making the poet's fear of criticism vivid.
Pindar states a general truth about teaching and experience, implicitly praising Melesias's expertise.
Alkimedon's victory is said to renew his grandfather, giving vigour against old age, a striking claim of rejuvenating glory.
Fame is made a daughter of Hermes who carries news to the dead, giving the abstract idea a messenger's role.
